sections.html:
Choosing the right Arizona notice starts with the reason: rent not paid, a lease violation, a health and safety violation, a breach that can't be repaired, or a periodic tenancy that's simply ending. The statute assigns a different count of days to each, and a landlord who grabs the wrong one risks losing the case.

Reason for the noticeHow long the tenant has
Unpaid rent5 days after written notice
Material lease breachEnds no sooner than 10 days after receipt if not fixed in 10 days
Health and safety breach under 33-1341Ends no sooner than 5 days after receipt if not fixed in 5 days
Material and irreparable breachImmediate termination notice
Month-to-month tenancy30 days before the rental date
Week-to-week tenancy10 days before the termination date

Inside A.R.S. 33-1368 the word days is defined as calendar days, which means Saturdays and Sundays are counted. The two periodic tenancy rules come from A.R.S. 33-1375.

sections.h2: What a five-day nonpayment notice must say
sections.html:
Three things belong in it. It's written, it states that rent hasn't been paid, and it warns that the landlord means to terminate the rental agreement unless the rent arrives within five days. Subsection 33-1368(B) supplies that language.

Timing matters too. A landlord has to wait until after the last day of the notice before filing. The court must dismiss the case if the tenant didn't get a proper termination notice with a chance to pay the rent and late fees, or if the notice wasn't served correctly.

Arizona doesn't dictate a form. Under A.R.S. 12-1175(D), no state agency or individual court may adopt or enforce a rule that makes a mandatory or technical form necessary for notices or pleadings in these cases, provided the notice meets the statutory content requirements.

sections.h2: How a notice is delivered and when it counts as received
sections.html:
Delivery rules are in A.R.S. 33-1313. A notice reaches the tenant when someone hands it over, or when it's mailed by registered or certified mail to the address the tenant designated, or to the last known residence when none was designated.

Mail adds a wrinkle. The tenant is considered to have received it on the date it truly arrives or five days after it was mailed, whichever is earlier. Since the 5-day and 10-day periods in 33-1368 run from receipt, a mailed notice lengthens the schedule.

For a clean record, many landlords hand-deliver and keep proof of it, or send certified mail and keep the receipt.

sections.h2: Ten-day and five-day lease breach notices
sections.html:
These notices give the tenant a chance to fix the problem, and if it's fixed in time the lease continues. The 10-day notice must describe the acts and omissions that make up the breach and state that the agreement ends on a date at least ten days after receipt if the breach isn't remedied within ten days.

A few details from the statute:

  • Material falsification on the rental application can be a breach, for example untrue information about occupants, pets, income or employment.
  • Falsification about criminal records, prior evictions or current criminal activity can't be cured under that section.
  • A five-day health and safety notice must be cured within five days. If repair or payment of damages fixes the breach before the date in the notice, the agreement doesn't end.
  • If the same or a similar health and safety problem returns during the lease after a cure, the landlord may file a special detainer action ten days after delivering written notice of the second noncompliance.

sections.h2: When a landlord can terminate immediately
sections.html:
Immediate termination is reserved for a breach that is both material and irreparable and that happens on the premises. The statute gives examples and says the list isn't exhaustive:

  • Illegal discharge of a weapon
  • Homicide, prostitution, or criminal street gang activity
  • Unlawful manufacturing, selling, using or storing of a controlled substance
  • Threatening or intimidating, or assault
  • Acts found to be a nuisance, or breaches that endanger the health, safety and welfare of the landlord, agent or another tenant, or involve imminent or actual serious property damage

After filing under A.R.S. 33-1377, the trial date and return date must be set no later than the third day after filing. If the court finds the breach occurred by a preponderance of the evidence, it must order restitution not less than 12 nor more than 24 hours later.

sections.h2: Ending a month-to-month tenancy before a sale
sections.html:
To close out a month-to-month tenancy, someone gives written notice at least 30 days ahead of the periodic rental date stated in it, and either the landlord or the tenant can do that. A week-to-week tenancy needs the written notice at least ten days before it ends.

A tenant who remains after the term ends, or after termination, without the landlord's consent exposes themselves to a possession suit. If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may also collect up to two months of periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is larger.

Consent in writing from the landlord changes the analysis, so any deal that lets a tenant stay past a sale belongs on paper.

sections.h2: How accepting rent can weaken a notice
sections.html:
Taking rent after a default can waive the right to terminate for that breach. A.R.S. 33-1371 provides that, apart from listed exceptions, accepting rent or any part of it while aware of a default waives the right to terminate for that breach.

A landlord needn't accept partial payment. One who does keeps the right to proceed only if the tenant agrees to the terms in a contemporaneous writing that includes a date when the balance is due. A housing assistance payment is treated differently: accepting it isn't accepting a partial payment and doesn't waive termination.

Before entering, a landlord owes the tenant at least two days' notice and must pick reasonable times. Emergencies, and situations where notice can't practically be given, are exceptions. The rule is A.R.S. 33-1343.

That statute also says the tenant can't unreasonably refuse consent when the landlord wants to show the unit to prospective or actual purchasers. In return, access can't be misused to harass the tenant, and the landlord has no other way in except a court order, the abandonment rules, or surrender of the premises.

Planning to sell a rented house? Build your showing schedule around the two-day minimum and keep a written log of every notice you give.

Raising rent, reducing services or threatening to sue for possession in response to a tenant's complaint is retaliation, and it's off limits. A.R.S. 33-1381 covers complaints to a housing or building code agency about a health and safety violation, complaints made to the landlord under 33-1324, and joining a tenants' union.

Six months is the line that matters. If the tenant complained within six months before the landlord acted, the law presumes retaliation. The landlord keeps the right to sue when rent is in default, or when the code violation came mostly from the tenant's own lack of reasonable care.

faqs.q: How many days is an eviction notice in Arizona?
faqs.a: It depends on the reason: five days for unpaid rent after written notice, ten days for a curable lease breach, five days for a health and safety breach, and an immediate notice for a material and irreparable breach. A month-to-month tenancy needs 30 days.

faqs.q: Do weekends count toward the five-day notice?
faqs.a: Yes. For A.R.S. 33-1368, days means calendar days.

faqs.q: Can a landlord evict without a written notice?
faqs.a: For nonpayment and lease breaches the statute calls for written notice. The case must be dismissed if the tenant wasn't given a proper notice and a chance to pay.

faqs.q: Does a landlord have to use a particular form?
faqs.a: No. A.R.S. 12-1175(D) bars courts and state agencies from requiring a mandatory or technical form, as long as the notice meets the statutory content requirements.

faqs.q: Can a landlord show the house to buyers while it is tenant-occupied?
faqs.a: Yes, with at least two days' notice at reasonable times, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent. Emergencies and impracticable situations are excepted.
